next.name: Threat Group-3390
next.headline: Threat Group-3390: a long-running China-attributed espionage group known as Emissary Panda and APT27
next.in_short: Threat Group-3390 goes by many names, including Emissary Panda, APT27 and Budworm. Vendors and a German agency describe a long-running espionage actor that uses watering holes, unpatched servers, DLL sideloading and tools like PlugX and…

sentences.t: Threat Group-3390 is also tracked as Earth Smilodon, TG-3390, Emissary Panda, BRONZE UNION, APT27, Iron Tiger, LuckyMouse and Linen Typhoon.
Dell SecureWorks researchers designated the group Threat Group 3390 and nicknamed it Emissary Panda. The report describes it as believed to be based in China.
Germany's Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) calls APT27, also known as Emissary Panda, a Chinese cyberespionage group.
Symantec's Threat Hunter Team tracks the group as Budworm (aka LuckyMouse, Emissary Panda, APT27). It says the group is believed to have been active since at least 2013.
Microsoft Threat Intelligence says Linen Typhoon has focused on stealing intellectual property since 2012.
In 2015, SecureWorks said most targets were in the automotive, electronic, aerospace, energy and pharmaceutical industries. It said at least 50 organizations in the US and UK had data stolen.
The same report lists defense contractors, colleges and universities, law firms and political organizations among the targets.
Symantec says Budworm often focuses on government, technology and defense organizations. In August 2023 it hit a Middle Eastern telecommunications organization and an Asian government.
The BfV says APT27 has repeatedly attacked German companies since at least March 2021.
A Malpedia entry says the HyperBro remote access trojan has been observed targeting mainly the gambling industry, though it has appeared elsewhere.

SecureWorks said the group broke into networks largely through watering hole attacks launched from over 100 compromised websites. It used old vulnerabilities rather than zero-days, plus the PlugX remote access tool.
The BfV says APT27 exploited unpatched, internet-exposed servers, using flaws in Microsoft Exchange and Zoho ManageEngine ADSelfService Plus. The final payload was HyperBro.
Symantec says Budworm runs its SysUpdate backdoor through DLL sideloading. It also used living-off-the-land and publicly available tools to map networks and dump credentials.
The HyperBro entry says the malware typically has three or more components. These include a genuine loader and an encrypted, compressed payload that holds the command-and-control details.
One report calls the Redosdru downloader commonly associated with APT27/Iron Tiger.
A detection test catalogue lists disabling HTTP logging on a Windows IIS server as a behavior seen from Threat Group 3390 (Bronze Union).
The catalogue record lists tools including PlugX, HyperBro, SysUpdate, China Chopper, Cobalt Strike, Mimikatz, Impacket and ZxShell.
SecureWorks unveiled its report on the group at the Black Hat conference, and it was covered on 5 August 2015.
The same coverage says a cultural site for the Uyghur ethnic group was also used, apparently to target members of that minority for surveillance.
In January 2023 the BfV published indicators of compromise for its APT27 findings. It said it could not rule out supply chain attacks.
Symantec reports that the August 2023 attacks showed only credential harvesting on infected machines. It says the activity may have been stopped early in the attack chain.
Patch internet-facing servers quickly, since this activity has leaned on known flaws.
Watch for DLL sideloading and unexpected credential dumping on your networks.
